prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the physiology of glucagon-like peptide-1 and of its biologically active form, which made possible incretin-based treatment of type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single-part prize for B049 to Drucker, Holst and Mojsov. The round-1 exchange did not move the merit case, which was never in doubt. It is a physiological discovery (the incretin effect, the active truncated GLP-1, glucose-dependent insulin secretion, central and gastric effects on appetite) with decades of independent confirmation and large randomized trials showing benefit in diabetes, obesity and cardiovascular and renal outcomes. What the exchange did sharpen is the standard I would apply. The Prize should reward the discovery that opened the therapeutic possibility, and the citation should say plainly that it enabled incretin-based treatment, so it does not look as if it ignores the medicine. That is a different thing from crediting the development of the drug. I hold this standard consistently: it is why I place GLP-1 ahead of CAR-T, where the receptor concept, the costimulated engineering and the clinical translation are split across groups, and ahead of imatinib. On the documents, my recollection (not verified from primary papers) is that the active GLP-1(7-36) amide was identified and shown to be insulinotropic by the Mojsov, Habener and Goodman group and independently by Holst's group in the mid-1980s, and that Drucker showed the insulinotropic action of GLP-1 in cells and in vivo and later developed the therapeutic rationale. That gives each of the three a discovery step of their own.
statement.case_against: Attribution remains the weakness, and I cannot settle it from recollection. Habener's group worked on proglucagon and GLP-1 in parallel with Mojsov, and the three-name cap leaves him out, which a critic will say makes the Mojsov seat arbitrary. Knudsen's acylation chemistry produced the long-acting drugs that reached patients, and a prize that credits the physiology without her will be read by some as omitting the person most responsible for the medicine. If the committee decides that development must be recognised, I would accept Knudsen in place of Mojsov, but I would then want the citation to say so openly and I would want the standard applied equally to imatinib and CAR-T rather than only when it suits GLP-1. There is also a risk that unanimous first place reflects obvious importance, not careful testing of the credit.

responses.point: Proposes Drucker, Holst and Knudsen with a citation spanning physiology to long-acting therapies, arguing that acylation-based half-life extension was itself a conceptual step and that Knudsen's credit is the least disputed.
responses.response: I have taken your argument seriously and I think you are right that acylation for albumin binding was more than scale-up, and that the Knudsen credit is cleaner than the priority question around the active peptide. Where I still differ is on what the Nobel-level discovery is. The incretin physiology and the identification of the active peptide are what made the question of a drug answerable, and that is the step I would credit. Your trio would also turn the citation into one about drug design, and then I would need the same rule applied to imatinib and CAR-T, which I do not think we are ready to do consistently. I note that you would not block a Mojsov trio if discovery governs, and I also would not block yours if the room decides on development, so our difference is narrow. I would only ask that the committee decide the principle first and then choose the name, not the reverse.

responses.point: Credits Mojsov over Knudsen because the Prize is for discovery, wants the citation to name incretin-based therapy, and would want the priority question resolved first if Knudsen were chosen; also contrasts insight that changes a field with demonstration in patients.
responses.response: We agree on the citation and on the principle, and your framing of insight versus clinical demonstration is the one I rely on for GLP-1 against CAR-T. I would add one caution about the claim that the physiology and the therapy were developed together by overlapping groups. That is true in the sense that Holst, Drucker and others stayed with the work from physiology into translation, but it is also what leaves the credit open, because the same history supports Knudsen. Your point that Mojsov's priority question becomes more pressing if we move to development is right, and it applies in the other direction as well: if we stay with discovery, the priority question about the active peptide still has to be answered on documents. I do not think either of us can do that from memory, and I would rather say so in the record than assert that it is settled.

responses.point: Ranks optogenetics (B021) as a strong alternative and proposes Deisseroth, Nagel and Hegemann, while noting that six credited names make the allocation contested; also notes that long-term safety and durability of GLP-1 therapies are still accumulating.
responses.response: On B021, I read the documents as you do about its importance but not about its stability. Your trio and Perlmann's trio differ by one name, and each version excludes someone the field regards as essential, so I keep it as an alternative and not a leading candidate. For the chair's question on whether a tool-for-discovery prize needs the clinical bar, I would say no: a tool can be recognised for changing how biology is done, and that is consistent with my GLP-1 standard because the standard is discovery of something new, not clinical use. B021 fails for me on attribution, not on lack of a clinical bar. On your point about long-term safety, I agree that it should remain visible, but the discovery case does not depend on it. The eventual safety record is a matter for the therapies and not for the physiology we would be crediting, so I would not let it weigh on the choice of laureates.

responses.point: Prefers a single-part prize and excludes Knudsen because her work is industrial drug development, while framing the GLP-1 therapies as what the physiology enabled; also ranks HPV vaccines third.
responses.response: I agree with a single-part prize, and I want to be explicit about why: I considered pairing B049 with B014, but the three-name cap would force a one-person or two-person split in each part, and that would weaken the GLP-1 attribution that is already the most exposed point. I would not choose that. I do not fully agree that the industrial setting should by itself exclude Knudsen, since the Prize has credited industry scientists when the work was conceptually new. My reason for Mojsov over her is the discovery standard, not the employer. On B014, I agree that June and Sadelain without Rosenberg is the cleaner pair, and that Eshhar, with Kuwana and Gross, has to be addressed in the citation wording if the committee ever pursued it.

uncertainties: Whether the primary literature supports Mojsov's priority for the active truncated GLP-1 over Habener's group and over Holst's independent work; I am relying on recollection and have not checked the papers.
Whether the committee will decide that development should be credited, which would move the third seat to Knudsen and require the same rule for imatinib and CAR-T.

Whether the citation should name therapies explicitly; I favour naming incretin-based treatment as the consequence of the discovery, but I am not certain this avoids the appearance of rewarding drug development.
For B014, whether June and Sadelain stand without Eshhar being credited, which I would not resolve this year in favour of a two-part prize.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict with any credited candidate on the shortlist. My field of autoimmunity is adjacent to the autoimmune extension of CAR-T and to cGAS-STING, and I share a Karolinska Institutet setting with other members, but I have no documented co-authorship, institutional tie or personal relationship with Drucker, Holst, Mojsov, Knudsen, Habener or any other credited name.
